prompt:
Write an essay of about 800 words on the subject below.

Write it the way an excellent, idiosyncratic human essayist would: someone with real expertise and strong opinions, writing in the first person for their own blog. Commit to a specific thesis that a thoughtful reader might disagree with. Use concrete particulars (names, numbers, incidents, things only someone who had done the work would know) in place of general statements. Vary sentence length. No headings, no bullet points, no summary paragraph at the end, and none of the stock phrases of AI writing.

Output only the essay, with no title.

Subject: an essay reviewing a book you think is underrated
raw:
Every few months someone tells me, with the glow of a convert, that they have finally read *Stoner*. I nod. I have stopped arguing. But what I want to say, and usually don't, is that they have read the wrong John Williams book, and that the one they should have read sits two spines over on the same shelf, in the same NYRB Classics livery, and almost nobody touches it.

*Augustus* won the National Book Award in 1973. It shared the prize with John Barth's *Chimera*, which tells you something about the era's divided taste, and it is the only time Williams was recognized in his lifetime by anyone other than his students in Denver. *Stoner* sold about two thousand copies on publication and then went quiet for forty-odd years. It came back by way of a French translation by Anna Gavalda, turned into a European phenomenon, and became Waterstones Book of the Year in 2013. That revival is a lovely story, and I believe it has distorted how we read Williams. We have taken his most consoling book for his best one.

Here is my claim, stated as plainly as I can: *Augustus* is the greater novel, and *Stoner*'s popularity rests partly on the fact that it flatters its readers in a way *Augustus* refuses to.

*Stoner* is about a man whose life looks like a failure from the outside and turns out, on inspection, to have been a quiet dignity all along. I love it. I have cried at the end of it, at the book slipping from his fingers. But think about who reads literary fiction in 2026 and why that story lands. It tells a great many people that their obscure, unrewarded devotion to something is its own vindication. It is the novel equivalent of being told you have a beautiful soul. *Augustus* tells you nothing of the kind. It is about a man who got everything, the whole known world, and spent fifty years discovering what it cost and who paid.

The book is epistolary, and that sounds dusty until you see what Williams does with it. Books One and Two are a mass of invented letters, memoirs, military dispatches, and senate records. There are letters from Maecenas, from Cicero, from Agrippa, from Livia, and gossip from people whose names you half-remember from a Latin class you didn't enjoy. Octavius himself barely speaks. For two-thirds of the novel you only see the most powerful man in history reflected in other people's fear, love, contempt, and calculation. He is a shape made out of rumors. Then, in Book Three, Williams finally hands him the pen. Augustus writes a long letter to Nicolaus of Damascus in the year 14, aboard a ship, near the end of his life. The voice you have been circling for three hundred pages turns out to be tired, lucid, and devastatingly unsentimental about himself.

I don't know another novel that withholds its protagonist so long and makes the withholding the point. Power, Williams is saying, is the condition of being known only through what others need you to be. Augustus says as much, more or less, near the end. He has become the "Rome" in other people's mouths, and the man has mostly evaporated.

The middle section is where people who have read it tend to go quiet when you mention it. Book Two belongs largely to Julia, Augustus's daughter, writing a journal from her exile on Pandateria, a rock off the Campanian coast where her father sent her in 2 BC for adultery that was probably also politics. Williams gives her the best prose in the book. She is witty and bitter, and she understands her father better than any senator does. She also understands that he loved her and destroyed her for the same reason, because the state required a symbol of moral renewal and his own household had to provide one. *Stoner* has its Edith, a wife rendered almost entirely as an obstacle, and I have always found her the weakest thing in it. Julia is what Williams could do when he let a woman think on the page. It makes me wish he had written ten more novels instead of the four he finished.

The objection I hear is that historical fiction is a lesser mode, costume drama with footnotes. Williams anticipated this. His author's note admits flatly that some documents are invented and some chronology has been bent. He wasn't writing about Rome in the way Robert Graves was, with a wink and a poisoned fig. He used Rome the way *Stoner* uses the University of Missouri, as a frame tight enough that the people inside it can't escape each other. The difference is scale. A tenure dispute and a civil war turn out to obey the same grammar of ambition and loyalty and betrayal, and *Augustus* is the book where he proved it.

What I can't get past is the last letter. An old man who ended the Republic, built the empire, exiled his only child, and buried nearly every heir he chose, sits on a ship and tries to tell one friend the truth. He doesn't ask to be forgiven or claim his work was worth it. He simply sets out what he did, the way a craftsman might list his tools.

I'd trade the falling book in Stoner's hands for that letter. I don't expect many people to agree, and I suspect that's part of why the book stays on the shelf.
